repos.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
repos.paper_summary:
Graph RAG is a method for answering global questions over large text corpora by using an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph and pre-generate hierarchical community summaries. The pipeline extracts entities and relationships from source text chunks, partitions the resulting graph into communities using the Leiden algorithm, and summarizes each community. At query time, it generates partial answers from community summaries in parallel and synthesizes them into a final response. This differs from standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which retrieves local text chunks and fails on corpus-wide sensemaking questions.

The authors evaluated Graph RAG against naïve RAG and a map-reduce baseline that summarizes raw source texts directly. They used two datasets of approximately 1 million tokens and 125 LLM-generated sensemaking questions per dataset. An LLM-as-a-judge assessed answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness. Global approaches outperformed naïve RAG, with comprehensiveness win rates between 72% and 83%. Intermediate-level community summaries provided better comprehensiveness and diversity than source-text summarization while using 26–33% fewer context tokens. Root-level summaries reduced token usage by over 97% compared to source-text processing. Limitations include evaluation on only two specific datasets and question types, with no validation of fabrication rates or end-user utility.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RAG cannot answer corpus-wide sensemaking questions, so GraphRAG builds an entity graph with community summaries and outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers graph-based retrieval, hierarchical summaries and benchmarks oriented toward explicit fact retrieval rather than global questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects Leiden communities, summarizes them, and answers queries by map-reduce over summaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare six conditions on two corpora of about one million tokens, using generated global sensemaking questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Global GraphRAG conditions beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness at 72-83% win rates on podcast transcripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation covers only two corpora and lacks a fabrication-rate comparison, which the authors name as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Root-level community summaries give a data index that beats vector RAG and competes with other global methods at lower token cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extraction prompts, self-reflection gleaning, community detection, context window tests, an example comparison, and system prompts.

repos.title: Step-DPO: Step-wise Preference Optimization for Long-chain Reasoning of LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Step-DPO is a preference optimization method for large language models that treats individual reasoning steps, rather than full answers, as the unit of comparison to improve mathematical reasoning. The method modifies the standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective by conditioning on preceding correct steps and optimizing the probability of the next correct step versus the first erroneous step. This allows the model to pinpoint specific errors in long chains of thought without penalizing earlier correct logic.

The authors construct a dataset of 10K preference pairs using a three-step pipeline: collecting incorrect model outputs, localizing the first error, and sampling self-generated corrections from the reference model. They find that using in-distribution data generated by the model itself yields better results than out-of-distribution data written by humans or GPT-4. On the MATH benchmark, applying Step-DPO to Qwen2-72B-Instruct increases accuracy from 69.4% to 70.8%, while GSM8K accuracy rises from 92.4% to 94.0%. These gains are achieved with fewer than 500 training steps. The approach also improves performance on competition-level problems like AIME 2024, where Qwen2-72B-Instruct scores 4/30 compared to 5/30 for the base instruct model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Vanilla DPO cannot locate errors in long math reasoning, so Step-DPO compares individual reasoning steps instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods improve math reasoning through prompting, data augmentation or reinforcement learning, but each has stated limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Step-DPO
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO builds preference pairs from the first wrong step, with the model's own correct continuation as the preferred choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO raises Qwen2-72B-Instruct to 70.8% on MATH, with approximately a 3% boost for models above 70B.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude Step-DPO with 10K pairs gives significant gains, particularly for large models.

repos.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
repos.paper_summary: Harness2 is a plug-and-play framework for recursive agent harnessing. It refines an LLM agent's execution harness (its prompts, memory, skills, tools, and related components) for each task, and it updates a separate improvement harness across tasks. Task-level recursion uses a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step. It proposes harness edits, runs them under matched conditions against a reference execution, and composes only changes supported by behavioral contrasts, without a ground-truth verifier. Parallel recursion composes from a pool of candidates, and sequential recursion chains revisions. Both are controlled by a budget k. After each task, reflection adds adopted harnesses and supported lessons to a library that guides later proposals. On WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and LAB (Partial pass rate), with Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 under OpenCode and Codex, one step improves every configuration by up to 11.5 points, 4.5 points, and 11.8 percentage points. Parallel recursion at k=5 adds up to 3.9, 4.2, and 6.7 more. The authors state that probe contrasts are limited by execution stochasticity and shared model biases, and that adopted harnesses are not verified to be optimal.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 targets open-world agent harness evolution, which lacks ground-truth verifiers and fails to transfer across tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness2
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 pairs task-level recursion, which refines the current harness without verifiers, with a library that carries lessons to later tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Single-step Harness2 exceeds the base harness on all three benchmarks for GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash under both initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Score gains grow with recursion budget, and each ablated component lowers WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 differs from prior harness optimization by learning from its own refinements across a task stream without ground-truth feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 turns task-specific refinement into reusable experience, with gains reported across three benchmarks, two executors, and two initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers comparison criteria, benchmark splits, baselines, tool-call errors, production harness comparison, failure cases, limitations, and prompts.

repos.title: Attention Is All You Need
repos.paper_summary:
The Transformer is a sequence transduction model that replaces recurrent and convolutional layers with multi-head self-attention. The architecture consists of six encoder and six decoder stacks, each containing sub-layers for scaled dot-product attention and position-wise feed-forward networks. Positional information is injected via fixed sinusoidal encodings added to token embeddings.

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German task, the large variant achieves 28.4 BLEU, exceeding previous best ensembles by over 2.0 BLEU. For English-to-French, it reaches 41.8 BLEU after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs. A base configuration requires only 12 hours of training on the same hardware. The model also generalizes to English constituency parsing, achieving 92.7 F1 in a semi-supervised setting. Limitations include quadratic computational complexity relative to sequence length and reliance on beam search during inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Recurrent models process positions sequentially, which limits parallelization; the authors propose the Transformer, which uses only attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior convolutional models need operations that grow with distance between positions; the Transformer reduces this to a constant number.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: The model stacks six encoder and decoder layers built on scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, with sinusoidal positional encodings.

digest_headlines.heading: Why Self-Attention
digest_headlines.headline: Self-attention needs a constant number of sequential operations and a constant maximum path length, versus linear for recurrent layers.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Models trained on WMT 2014 data with Adam and a warmup learning-rate schedule, using dropout and label smoothing.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: The big Transformer scores 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, above prior results including ensembles, and generalizes to parsing.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the Transformer trains faster than recurrent or convolutional models and plan to extend it to other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix shows layer-5 encoder attention heads tracking long-distance verb dependencies, anaphora, and sentence structure.

repos.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary: Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting is a zero-shot prompting strategy for large language models that instructs the model to devise a plan dividing a task into subtasks before executing them. The extended variant, PS+, adds instructions to extract relevant variables and calculate intermediate results. On ten datasets covering arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning using GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT by an average of 6.3% on arithmetic tasks, reaching 76.7% accuracy compared to 70.4%. It also exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought on five of six arithmetic benchmarks. Error analysis on GSM8K shows PS+ reduces calculation errors from 7% to 5% and missing-step errors from 12% to 7%, though semantic misunderstanding errors remain at 27%. The paper notes two limitations: prompt sensitivity requires careful manual design, and the method does not address semantic understanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot chain-of-thought errors are split into calculation, missing-step, and semantic errors, and a plan-based prompt targets two of them.

digest_headlines.heading: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
digest_headlines.headline: Plan-and-Solve prompting uses a zero-shot trigger that asks the model to devise and carry out a plan, followed by an answer-extraction prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use ten benchmarks with text-davinci-003 and compare against zero-shot and few-shot baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on all arithmetic datasets and averages 76.7 against 77.6 for Manual-CoT.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places Plan-and-Solve among chain-of-thought methods that use zero-shot prompting and planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that plan-based zero-shot prompting outperforms Zero-shot-CoT and matches few-shot CoT on some arithmetic datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Prompt design is labour-intensive and the method does not address semantic misunderstanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The paper lists the datasets and their licences and states that the prompts contain no personal information or discriminatory wording.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists trigger-sentence ablations for every dataset and example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+.

repos.title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
repos.paper_summary: DeepTutor is an open-source agentic tutoring framework that combines citation-grounded problem tutoring with difficulty-calibrated question generation, both driven by a shared learner model. Its Hybrid Personalization Engine pairs Static Knowledge Grounding (knowledge-graph traversal plus dense search, fused by reciprocal rank fusion) with Dynamic Personal Memory, a trace forest of past interactions. Three memory agents query this forest and update a learner profile after each session. Tutoring proceeds through investigation, guided solving, and evidence-based writing. Question generation selects ideas, then a separate validator checks each question, answer, and explanation. TutorBench covers five university-level disciplines, with learner profiles tied to course material and evaluated by an LLM student simulator and rubric-based assessors. DeepTutor improves personalized metrics by 10.8% on average, and a solver-only transfer study shows a 29.4% average gain across five backbone models. Human raters and the LLM judge show aligned preference trends. Stated limitations include simulated rather than real learners, no large-scale human student study, and added inference cost. The Book Engine and Partners are described architecturally without learner-outcome evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing tutoring and question-generation workflows run in isolation, so tutoring traces do not shape later practice items.

digest_headlines.heading: DeepTutor Framework
digest_headlines.headline: A shared personalization engine feeds problem tutoring and question generation, and every completed interaction updates the learner profile.

digest_headlines.heading: Extending the Personalization Substrate
digest_headlines.headline: Extensions such as Deep Research, Mastery Path and the Book Engine reuse one personalization substrate, while quantitative evaluation covers only the tutoring core.

digest_headlines.heading: TutorBench
digest_headlines.headline: TutorBench pairs 90 learner profiles from 30 knowledge bases in five disciplines with 270 source-grounded interactive tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: DeepTutor reaches 3.91 overall quality on TutorBench against 3.53 for the Naive Tutor baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers LLM memory, knowledge tracing and LLM tutors, and finds adaptive tutoring on individualized materials underexplored.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DeepTutor improves overall quality by 10.8% on TutorBench and yields a 29.4% average gain across five backbone families.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive results rest on LLM simulators and rubric judges, and the extensions' effects on real learners remain untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extended related work, implementation details, TutorBench construction, evaluation protocol, hyperparameters and backbone models.

repos.title: Gradio: Hassle-Free Sharing and Testing of ML Models in the Wild
repos.paper_summary:
Gradio is an open-source Python package that generates a web-based interface for machine learning models, allowing non-technical users to test them via a shared URL. The system supports inputs and outputs for images, text, and audio, and is compatible with Scikit-Learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or arbitrary Python functions. When a researcher launches the interface, Gradio creates an SSH tunnel to host the model on the original machine, enabling remote collaborators to access it through a browser without installing software. Users can manipulate inputs, such as cropping or occluding image regions, and flag incorrect predictions to send feedback directly to the developer.

The authors validated the tool in a pilot study involving an ML researcher and a cardiologist classifying echocardiograms for pacemaker presence. The underlying model achieved an AUC of 0.93. Setup took approximately 10 minutes. During testing, the cardiologist successfully identified model failures by flipping images vertically and used the built-in tools to verify predictions by occluding the pacemaker. Limitations include the study's small scope of one user pair over a short period, and the absence of quantitative measures for trust or satisfaction.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Domain experts usually cannot try ML models during development, so the authors built Gradio, a Python package that generates web interfaces.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Interviews with 12 ML researchers yielded four design requirements for interfaces, sharing, input manipulation, and notebook embedding.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: Gradio wraps a trained model in an Interface object with four required parameters and shares it through a secure tunnel.

digest_headlines.heading: Pilot Study: Echocardiogram Classification
digest_headlines.headline: A single pilot pair found the shared link let a cardiologist probe a pacemaker classifier and flag failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion & Next Steps
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the package to widen domain expert access, but a single short pair study cannot establish usefulness.

repos.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
repos.paper_summary: FlashAttention is an exact attention algorithm that reduces GPU memory traffic by tiling the computation to avoid materializing the full $N \times N$ attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). It computes softmax incrementally over blocks of keys and values loaded into on-chip SRAM, storing only normalization statistics for the backward pass. The paper proves FlashAttention requires $\Theta(N^2 d^2 M^{-1})$ HBM accesses, where $d$ is head dimension and $M$ is SRAM size, compared to $\Theta(Nd + N^2)$ for standard attention, establishing a lower bound showing no exact algorithm can asymptotically improve this for all $M$. On GPT-2 with sequence length 1024, it achieves a 7.6x speedup over PyTorch attention. End-to-end training yields a 15% speedup on BERT-large versus MLPerf 1.1 records, a 3x speedup on GPT-2 versus HuggingFace baselines, and a 2.4x speedup on Long-Range Arena. Longer contexts enabled by FlashAttention improve GPT-2 perplexity by 0.7 and achieve better-than-chance accuracy on Path-X (61.4%) and Path-256 (63.1%). Limitations include the need for custom CUDA kernels for each new attention variant and lack of support for multi-GPU IO optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Attention is quadratic in sequence length, and making it IO-aware reduces slow GPU memory accesses while keeping results exact.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: GPU attention is memory-bound, and standard attention writes the N by N score and probability matrices to HBM.

digest_headlines.heading: FlashAttention: Algorithm, Analysis, and Extensions
digest_headlines.headline: Tiling and recomputation give exact attention with fewer HBM accesses, and a lower bound limits any exact algorithm.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: FlashAttention trains BERT-large 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record and GPT-2 up to 3x faster than HuggingFace.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations are that each attention variant needs its own low-level GPU kernel and that multi-GPU data transfer is not analyzed.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, backward-pass derivations, algorithm details, proofs, extensions and full benchmark tables.

repos.title: ResearchStudio-Reel: Automate the Last Mile of Research from Paper to Poster, Video, and Blog
repos.paper_summary:
ResearchStudio-Reel is a set of five skills, runnable in Claude Code and Codex, that turns one paper PDF into an editable PowerPoint poster, a narrated talk video with a PowerPoint deck, and a bilingual Word blog. A shared extractor, Paper2Assets, builds one bundle of text, cleaned figures, metadata, and section IDs that all three generators read, so none of them re-parses the PDF. Paper2Poster uses a measured-fill loop that scores each section's fill ratio, edits sections until they fall between 0.90 and 0.98, and requires figures to fill at least 90% of their card. Paper2Reel then links poster regions, video segments, and blog passages in one HTML viewer.

On the 100-paper Paper2Poster benchmark, the Claude Code configuration has the best scores among automated systems on all three aesthetic sub-criteria and the best or tied-best on two of three information sub-criteria. Under two VLM judges, its average aesthetic score is 3.56 versus 3.03 for the authors' posters, and it wins overall on 74 and 95 of the 100 papers.

The paper states that its evaluative, generative, and architectural limits remain to be studied. The provided text reports no quantitative evaluation for the video or blog artifacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Paper-to-poster, video, and blog tools mostly stay artifact-specific, so the paper proposes an editable, linked workspace for all three.

digest_headlines.heading: Skills
digest_headlines.headline: Five skills share one extracted bundle, with three generators feeding a single interactive viewer that keeps sections aligned.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the 100-paper benchmark, the Claude Code configuration scores 3.56 on aesthetics against the authors' 3.03.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications
digest_headlines.headline: Three intended users, an individual author, a lab, and a course, would run the same pipeline at different cadences.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior paper-to-poster, video, and blog systems each target one output, while this work binds editable artifacts into one linked viewer.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation relies on proxy measures, and the pipeline cannot yet create new method or overview diagrams.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Editable, linked artifacts are delivered, with posters above the authors' own on aesthetics under two judges.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists failure modes, scope limits, ethics, reproducibility, per-judge scores, comparisons, a gallery, and the baseline prompt.

repos.title: Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs
repos.paper_summary: Faiss is an open-source library that accelerates similarity search on GPUs by implementing a register-based $k$-selection algorithm, WarpSelect, and optimized layouts for brute-force and product quantization (PQ) based searches. WarpSelect maintains intermediate state entirely in GPU registers to avoid memory bottlenecks, using odd-size sorting networks to merge per-lane queues with a shared warp queue. This design achieves up to 55% of theoretical peak performance and makes nearest neighbor search 8.5 times faster than prior GPU implementations. The library applies these kernels to exact brute-force search, IVFADC approximate search, and compressed-domain PQ search. On the Yfcc100M dataset, it constructs a high-accuracy $k$-NN graph over 95 million images in 35 minutes. It builds a graph connecting 1 billion vectors in under 12 hours using four Maxwell Titan X GPUs. The implementation supports vector dimensions up to 64 sub-vectors for PQ codes. Limitations include reliance on specific NVIDIA hardware features like warp shuffles and a requirement that input data fits within the GPU’s global memory or be streamed efficiently from host memory.
